notes: Every reaction the game can cast. Enthalpies are standard values at 25 °C and 1 atm, computed from standard enthalpies of formation in the NIST Chemistry WebBook (H2O(g) -241.826, H2O(l) -285.830, CO2(g) -393.51, CH4(g) -74.87 kJ/mol). Each entry needs a reviewer before it ships to classrooms.

reactions.name: Conjure Water (hydrogen burns)
reactions.concept: Synthesis: two gases join into water and release a lot of heat.
reactions.short_seedling: Two gases join and give off heat.
reactions.real_world: Hydrogen fuel cells and the main engines of the Space Shuttle used this reaction.
reactions.safety: Real hydrogen + oxygen mixtures explode violently; only trained chemists handle them.
reactions.source: NIST Chemistry WebBook, standard enthalpy of formation of H2O(g)

reactions.name: Split Water (electrolysis)
reactions.concept: Electricity can pull water apart into hydrogen and oxygen. It costs energy instead of releasing it.
reactions.short_seedling: Electricity splits water into two gases.
reactions.real_world: Green hydrogen plants split water with electricity from solar and wind.
reactions.source: NIST Chemistry WebBook, standard enthalpy of formation of H2O(l)

reactions.name: Fireball (methane burns)
reactions.concept: Combustion: a fuel joins with oxygen and makes carbon dioxide, water and heat.
reactions.short_seedling: Methane burns into CO2, water and heat.
reactions.real_world: This is the flame on a gas stove.
reactions.source: NIST Chemistry WebBook, standard enthalpies of formation of CH4, CO2 and H2O(g)

reactions.name: Burning wood (carbon burns)
reactions.concept: Fire needs fuel, oxygen and heat. Take any one away and it goes out.
reactions.short_seedling: Fire needs fuel, oxygen and heat.
reactions.real_world: Wood is mostly carbon compounds; in the game it is simplified to pure carbon.
reactions.source: NIST Chemistry WebBook, standard enthalpy of formation of CO2(g)

phase_changes.source: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, enthalpy of fusion of water
CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, enthalpy of vaporization of water at 100 °C

phase_changes.note: Why 2H2 + O2 -> 2H2O(g) releases 483.6 kJ but splitting 2H2O(l) costs 571.7 kJ: the difference, about 88 kJ (2 × 44.0 kJ/mol), is the heat it takes to turn liquid water into steam at 25 °C.
phase_changes.source: NIST Chemistry WebBook: standard enthalpies of formation H2O(g) -241.826 and H2O(l) -285.830 kJ/mol differ by 44.004 kJ/mol, the standard enthalpy of vaporization of water at 25 °C (CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics gives 44.0 kJ/mol)

phase_changes.note: Liquid nitrogen boils at 77.34 K (-195.8 °C, shown in game as -196 °C). Each mole that boils takes in about 5.6 kJ, which is how the Frost spell pulls heat out of what it touches.
phase_changes.source: NIST Chemistry WebBook, SRD 69, Nitrogen, phase change data (https://webbook.nist.gov/cgi/cbook.cgi?ID=C7727379&Mask=4): Tboil = 77.34 K (Jacobsen, Stewart, et al., 1986); enthalpy of vaporization 5.6 kJ/mol at 77 K (Giauque and Clayton, 1933)
